Forward-looking expected return for the D4/D5 30-year projection: each portfolio's own 30-year historical annualized return (Appendix C), applied forward as a constant. A worked Sharpe-ratio comparison: using Appendix C's 20-year return/stdev and Appendix D's risk-free-rate assumption (MA1), compute the 20-year Sharpe ratio for both portfolios by hand, showing arithmetic, displayed in a bar graph.

balance.argument_a: On the case's primary metric (20-year Sharpe ratio), Buffett's 90/10 Portfolio posts 0.6611 against All-Weather's 0.6600 -- essentially identical risk-adjusted efficiency. But Buffett 90/10 also carries a far higher raw annualized return at every single holding period in Appendix C (9.98% vs 7.40% at 30 years, 10.63% vs 6.74% at 20 years), which the D4 projection shows compounding into a dramatically larger 30-year nest egg. If risk-adjusted efficiency is genuinely a wash, the higher-return option is the one actually building more wealth for the same 'unit' of risk-adjusted return.
balance.argument_b: The All-Weather Portfolio matches Buffett 90/10's risk-adjusted efficiency (20-year Sharpe: 0.6600 vs 0.6611, a gap of roughly two-thousandths) while carrying under half the volatility (7.50% vs 13.83% 30-year standard deviation) and less than half the worst-case drawdown (-20.58% vs -45.52%). Benjamin has explicitly said he does not know how he would emotionally handle a severe portfolio drop -- if the risk-adjusted return really is a tie, the portfolio that protects against exactly the loss he is most afraid of, at no efficiency cost, is the stronger choice.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric (case.json.primary_metric, 20-year Sharpe ratio) per sensitivity_model.py's evaluate(): A(Buffett 90/10) = 0.6611, B(All-Weather) = 0.6600, margin 0.18%, Buffett fractionally ahead -- a genuine, sourced near-tie, well inside SPEC's 20% cap. The alternate lens (30-year projected terminal portfolio value) is NOT close (~55% margin, Buffett favored) -- kept out of case.md and out of this argument text per case-write's no-leaked-result rule; both readings are recorded in sensitivity_model.py and discussed in FACILITATOR.md.

derived.risk_free_rate_flex_flip: At risk_free_rate=0.75% (the -50% flex), the winner flips to All-Weather (0.7154 vs 0.7544); at the base 1.5% and the +50% flex (2.25%), Buffett 90/10 stays ahead. See sensitivity_model.py.

sensitivity_note: The primary metric (20-year Sharpe ratio, a 0.18% near-tie) is sensitive to Appendix D's MA1 risk-free-rate assumption -- P5's +/-50% sweep finds the winner CAN flip depending on that single assumed input. The D4/D5 30-year projection is a completely separate metric, not close (~55% margin, Buffett 90/10 favored), and is itself sensitive to MA2's forward-return assumption. See FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_model.py for both readings; neither the direction nor the threshold of either sensitivity appears anywhere in case.md.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No universally agreed convention exists for which risk-free rate a 30-year-old should assume when hand-computing a forward-looking Sharpe estimate over a multi-decade horizon; this is a genuine methodological choice, not a knowable fact that better research could pin down. P5's +/-50% sweep on Appendix D's MA1 (base 1.5%) finds the 20-year Sharpe-ratio winner CAN flip (verified in sensitivity_model.py and tier2_probes.py P5 output). Disclosed here, in FACILITATOR.md's Deep Conflict thread 1, and in the case's own Socratic questions -- never as a literal margin or winner in case.md.
